Managed Agents: the multiagent block

A coordinator works the same way on every platform. It delegates to subagents, and each subagent runs in an isolated context and returns only a condensed result (see the companion page on designing multi-agent systems). What changes from platform to platform is where you declare the coordinator, its specialists and the alternatives to subagents. In Claude Managed Agents, you declare them in the
block of the agent definition. With type
, subagents and dynamic workflows are both on by default, and you can also give the session an advisor.

The table below talks about threads, so one definition first. Each agent in a session runs in its own session thread: a context-isolated event stream with its own conversation history. The agent that the session runs reports in the primary thread, the session-level event stream, and every delegated agent gets an additional thread spawned at runtime. Whether a thread can be messaged again after its agent reports is what separates subagents from workflow runs.
The three ways a Managed Agents session can involve other agents
Approach
Who directs the work
Choose it when
Watch for
Subagents
The agent delegates and reads each report. A subagent's thread persists, so the agent can send follow-ups
The agent needs to follow up with a subagent, or needs listed specialists with their own system prompts and tools
Delegation is one level deep, with at most 25 child threads per session, idle ones included
Dynamic workflows
A program the agent writes runs many agents in phases in the background and combines their results
Most work that needs several agents: audits, migrations, deep research, cross-checking
No follow-ups to a run's threads, and every agent uses tokens, so set a session budget
Advisor
One agent does the work and consults an advisor model mid-turn
One agent should do the work, with stronger judgment at planning or final review
Only the primary thread can consult it, and consultations are billed at the advisor model's rates

You decide which of these the agent may use, and the agent decides when to use them. Steer that decision in the system prompt, for example by telling the agent when to start a workflow run. Predefined and inline agents, and the limits on them
Each subagent is either predefined or inline. A
predefined
agent is one you have already created and listed. It runs with its own model, system prompt, tools, MCP servers and skills. An
inline

agent isn't saved anywhere. The coordinator, or a workflow, defines it at the moment it hands out the work, and it uses the coordinator's model, tools, MCP servers and skills. Inline agents are on by default, so unless you turn them off, the coordinator can create helpers you never reviewed.
Predict first
An inline subagent needs access to the GitHub MCP server. Where do you declare that server so the inline agent can use it?

Inline agents have no definition of their own, so you can't use one to narrow their access. They take on the MCP servers and tools of the agent the session runs. To give a specialist tools the coordinator doesn't have, make it a predefined agent. Claude Code: subagents, agent teams or a dynamic workflow
Claude Code offers several ways to run work in parallel. Three of them are coordination patterns, and each one fits a different kind of work.
Choosing a coordination pattern in Claude Code
Pattern
What it is
Use it when
Subagents
Delegated workers inside one session that do a side task in their own context and return a summary
A side task would flood the main conversation with search results, logs or file contents you won't need again
Agent teams
Multiple coordinated sessions with a shared task list and inter-agent messaging, managed by a lead. Experimental and off by default
Claude should split a project into pieces, assign them, and keep the workers in sync
Dynamic workflows
A script that runs many subagents and cross-checks their results
The job outgrows a handful of subagents, or findings need to be verified against each other

The main difference is how the workers communicate. Subagents talk only to the session that started them, and each returns a single summary, so they suit isolated side tasks such as investigating one bug across dozens of files. Teammates in an agent team are peer sessions. They share a task list and message one another, which helps when pieces of a project depend on each other's progress. That shared state also brings back the coordination cost that subagents avoid. A dynamic workflow takes coordination out of the conversation entirely: a script runs the subagents and checks their results against each other, for jobs too big to manage one turn at a time. Agent teams are a Claude Code feature. They are experimental and must be turned on before use.
Apply it to your own work

Take a migration you might run across 200 files. Would you use a few subagents started from the conversation, an agent team, or a dynamic workflow? What about the job's size and its need for cross-checking decides it?
Checkpoint 5 of 5
Check yourself

In Claude Code, you want to find out why one test fails intermittently. That means reading CI logs and dozens of source files. You need only the root cause back, and the main conversation should stay focused on your feature work. Which coordination pattern fits?
A dynamic workflow, so a script runs the investigation and cross-checks the findings
An agent team, so a lead can assign the investigation to a teammate that shares a task list with the other sessions
Several subagents in a chain, each passing its findings to the next until one returns the root cause
A subagent, which investigates in its own context and returns a single summary to the session that started it
